captions: Part nine. Let's put it to work, and
pull out the lessons.
Using it takes a few lines.
Create a Memory object. The defaults are Qdrant,
OpenAI embeddings, and an OpenAI model, and every
piece is swappable.
After each turn, call add, with the messages
and a user id. That's the whole write
path.
Before answering, call search, with the question, a
filter for this user, and how many results
you want.
Then put the returned memories into your prompt.
Everything we've covered happens inside those two calls.
Running this in production raises a few more
questions.
Make writes asynchronous, so extraction never delays the
reply.
Give search a latency budget: it happens before
every answer.
Plan for deletion and privacy. Users will ask
to be forgotten, and expiry dates let stale
memories disappear on their own.
Track the cost per turn: at least one
LLM call and a few embeddings for every
write.
And evaluate on your own conversations. Benchmarks are
a starting point, not a guarantee.
So what does Mem0 teach about memory systems?
Distill, don't replay: extraction at write time buys
cheap reads.
Atomic facts are easier to match and deduplicate.
Make ids easy for LLMs to copy.
Hybrid retrieval beats pure vectors: semantic, keyword, and
entity signals each catch what the others miss.
Keep history, whether by invalidating edges or by
appending, so the timeline is never lost.
And scope everything, on every call.
Let's recap.
Memory is a system you build around a
stateless model.
The twenty twenty five design extracted facts, then
chose ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, or NOOP for each.
Vectors and HNSW find similar memories in milliseconds.
The graph variant added entities, invalidated edges, and
dual retrieval.
In the paper, Mem0 kept most of full
context's accuracy, at a fraction of its latency
and tokens.
The twenty twenty six design makes one add-only
call, links entities, and fuses three signals when
reading.
Good memory isn't remembering everything. It's remembering less,
but the right things. Thanks for watching.
